paragraphs.text: Spider silk has a reputation that is, for once, largely deserved. Weight for weight, the strongest silks are tougher than steel and many synthetic fibres, able to absorb a great deal of energy before breaking, and they are made at room temperature from water-based solutions rather than in factories that require high heat and harsh chemicals. For more than a century, people have tried to exploit this material, and for more than a century the attempts have run into the same obstacle: spiders are extremely difficult to farm. The obstacle has shaped the entire history of the subject.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: A single spider can produce several different kinds of silk, each from its own set of glands and each suited to a different purpose. The dragline silk on which a spider hangs and which forms the frame of a web is strong and relatively stiff; the capture spiral of an orb web is far more elastic and coated with sticky droplets; other silks wrap prey, line nests or protect eggs. The existence of so many types from one animal is part of what makes spider silk interesting to engineers, since it shows that small changes in the underlying proteins produce very different properties. Some species can produce as many as seven distinct silks, although most of them are used far less often than the dragline.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The secret of the strength of silk lies in its structure. The proteins that make it up contain regions that pack tightly into rigid crystals and regions that remain loose and tangled. The crystals provide strength, the tangled regions allow stretching, and the combination lets the fibre absorb the impact of a flying insect without snapping or throwing the insect back out. The way the spider spins matters as much as the protein: as the liquid silk passes along a narrowing duct, water is removed and the molecules are pulled into alignment, a process that researchers have found very hard to copy. Spiders can even adjust the properties of their silk by changing the speed at which they draw it out.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Farming spiders, the obvious solution, has repeatedly failed. Unlike silkworms, which live peacefully in large numbers and whose cocoons can be unwound, most spiders are solitary and territorial, and many will eat their neighbours if kept together. Each needs to be fed live prey, and the amount of silk collected from a single animal is tiny. In the early twentieth century a few enterprises attempted to produce spider silk commercially, and a celebrated textile was eventually woven from the silk of more than a million spiders, but it took years to make and served only as a curiosity. Silkworms, by contrast, have been domesticated for thousands of years and cannot survive in the wild.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The modern approach is to produce the proteins without the spider. The genes responsible for silk proteins have been inserted into bacteria, yeast, plants and even goats, whose milk then contained silk proteins that could be extracted. These methods do yield the proteins, but turning them into fibres as good as the natural ones has proved difficult. Silk genes are long and highly repetitive, which many host organisms handle poorly, and the artificial spinning processes developed so far produce fibres that are usually weaker than those of a spider, because they do not reproduce the conditions inside the spinning duct. Each host has advantages: bacteria are cheap to grow, while plants and animals can produce larger proteins.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Progress has nonetheless been steady. Some research groups have produced fibres whose strength approaches that of natural dragline silk by imitating the gradual changes in acidity and salt concentration that occur in the duct of the spider. Others have abandoned the goal of an exact copy and use silk proteins to make films, gels and coatings, where the precise fibre structure matters less. Silk proteins are generally well tolerated by the human body, and several of these materials are being tested for medical uses such as stitches and supports for repairing damaged tissue. Such applications need only small quantities, which makes the high cost of production less important.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Commercial products remain limited. A number of companies have announced clothing or sports equipment containing engineered silk, and some have reached small-scale production, but the cost remains high compared with conventional synthetic fibres, and the quantities made are small. Investors have at times been disappointed by how slowly the technology has developed. Researchers in the field tend to be more patient, pointing out that it took decades for synthetic fibres such as nylon to move from the laboratory to widespread use. Several start-up companies in the field have closed or changed direction.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Whatever the eventual commercial result, the study of spider silk has already changed how materials scientists think. The idea that a strong, tough material can be assembled from simple ingredients at ordinary temperatures, by controlling structure rather than by applying energy, has influenced research on other materials, from adhesives to composites. The spider, in this sense, has taught more than it has supplied, and that lesson may prove to be its most valuable contribution even if the dream of spider-silk cables and clothing is never fully realised. Nature, in other words, has already done the experiment.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: The public park, a large area of green space owned by a city and open to everyone free of charge, is a surprisingly recent invention. For most of history, the open spaces in and around towns were either common land used for grazing and gathering fuel, or private grounds belonging to royalty and the aristocracy, into which the public might be admitted on sufferance, at certain hours, if properly dressed. The idea that a city government should buy land, lay it out for recreation and maintain it at public expense for all its inhabitants took shape only in the first half of the nineteenth century. Even then, it was far from obvious that such spending was a proper use of public money.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The pressure came from rapid industrial growth. Cities that doubled or tripled in size within a few decades expanded over the fields and commons that had once lain within walking distance of their centres, and working people found themselves living in crowded districts with no open space at all. Reformers concerned with public health argued that fresh air and exercise were essential to prevent disease, while others worried about the moral effects of a population whose only leisure was the public house. Parks were promoted as a remedy for both problems. Mortality in the most crowded districts was far higher than in the surrounding countryside, and open space was one of the few remedies that seemed within reach.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Early parks were often paid for in unusual ways. Some were donated by wealthy industrialists, who gave land to their home towns and expected in return to be remembered as benefactors. Others were financed by selling plots for expensive houses around the edge of the park, on the reasonable assumption that buyers would pay more to overlook green space; the income from these sales covered the cost of the park itself. A few were created by public subscription, in which residents contributed money towards a shared purchase, though these rarely raised enough on their own. The houses built in this way are still among the most valuable properties in several cities.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The design of parks reflected ideas about what they were for. Landscape designers of the period favoured winding paths, lakes and carefully placed groups of trees intended to imitate the countryside and give city dwellers the sense of having escaped the streets. Formal flower beds, bandstands and glasshouses were added later, often in response to demand from visitors who wanted more to do than walk. Rules were strict: many early parks banned games, closed at dusk and employed keepers to enforce standards of behaviour that would now seem remarkable. Some parks even required visitors to be admitted by ticket in their first years.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Sport gradually changed the use of parks. By the end of the nineteenth century, organised games had become hugely popular among working people, and pressure grew for pitches, courts and playgrounds. Many authorities resisted at first, fearing damage to lawns and flower beds, but most eventually set aside areas for games, and some newer parks were designed around sports facilities from the start. The children’s playground, with fixed equipment such as swings, became common in the early twentieth century, promoted by campaigners who argued that children needed safe places to play away from traffic. Swimming pools and boating lakes followed in the larger parks.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: In the twentieth century, parks faced long periods of neglect. As cities spent more on housing, roads and other services, park budgets were often among the first to be cut, and the staff who had once maintained the grounds were reduced or removed entirely. Glasshouses decayed, lakes silted up and bandstands were demolished. By the 1980s many parks in older industrial cities were widely regarded as unsafe, and use declined, which in turn weakened the case for spending money on them. Some local authorities considered selling parts of their parks for development.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: A revival began towards the end of the century. Research linking access to green space with physical and mental health gave parks a new justification, and groups of local residents, often organised as friends of a particular park, began raising money, volunteering and lobbying for investment. Restoration schemes brought back lost features, and new parks were created on former industrial land, railway lines and docks. Some of the most admired recent examples occupy sites that would once have been considered entirely unsuitable for green space. Volunteer groups now carry out much of the routine work that paid staff once did.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The funding problem, however, has never been fully solved. Unlike schools or waste collection, parks are not usually a legal obligation for city governments, which makes their budgets vulnerable whenever money is short. Some cities have experimented with charitable trusts, sponsorship or income from events and cafés, each of which raises questions about whether a space meant for everyone can remain free and open while depending on commercial activity. The nineteenth-century reformers who created the public park would recognise the argument, since they faced a version of it themselves. What has changed is the evidence available to both sides. Parks, in other words, remain a public good whose value is easier to feel than to count.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should we grow genetically modified crops?

paragraphs.text: Few agricultural technologies have been argued about as fiercely as genetic modification. Crops whose genes have been altered in a laboratory, to resist insects, tolerate herbicides or survive drought, are grown on a large scale in some countries and heavily restricted in others, and public opinion is sharply divided. Much of the debate has been conducted as though the technology were a single thing to be accepted or rejected, when in practice it covers a wide range of changes with very different consequences. A sensible assessment has to begin by separating the questions that are often run together. They include questions of safety, of environmental effect, of ownership and of values.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first question is whether food from modified crops is safe to eat. Helen Achterberg, a food scientist, points out that major scientific bodies in many countries have reviewed the evidence and concluded that the approved varieties are as safe to eat as their conventional equivalents. She accepts that each new modification should be tested individually, since the safety of one does not guarantee the safety of another, but regards the general claim that modified food is dangerous as unsupported. In her view, the continuing public anxiety owes more to distrust of the companies involved than to the science.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The environmental effects are more complicated. Crops engineered to produce their own insecticide have allowed some farmers to reduce spraying substantially, which benefits other insects and the people applying the chemicals. On the other hand, crops designed to tolerate a particular weedkiller have encouraged heavy use of that product, and weeds resistant to it have spread across large areas. David Mwangi, an ecologist, argues that these outcomes depend less on the technology itself than on how it is managed, and that the same resistance problems arise whenever a single method of control is relied on too heavily. Rotating crops and weed-control methods, he says, would have prevented much of the resistance that has appeared.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Ownership is a separate and in some ways more serious concern. Modified seeds are usually patented, and farmers who buy them may be forbidden to save seed from their harvest for the following year, a practice that has been part of farming for thousands of years. Sofia Lindgren, who studies agricultural economics, notes that a small number of companies now control a large share of the world’s commercial seed supply, and that this concentration affects prices and the kinds of research that are funded. She does not regard the technology as the problem, but argues that its benefits have been shaped by the commercial arrangements through which it has been delivered.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Supporters emphasise what modification could achieve for poorer farmers. Varieties that tolerate drought, flooding or salty soil could protect harvests in regions where the climate is becoming less predictable, and crops enriched with vitamins could reduce deficiencies in diets that depend heavily on a single staple. Arjun Mehta, a plant breeder who has worked on such projects, observes that several of the most promising varieties have been developed by public research institutes rather than companies, and are intended to be distributed without patent restrictions. Their progress, he says, has been slowed more by regulation and public opposition than by technical difficulties. Critics respond that such varieties remain a small share of the modified crops actually grown.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Newer techniques have complicated the regulatory picture. Methods that make small, precise changes to the genes of a plant itself, without introducing genes from other species, can produce results that are indistinguishable from those of conventional breeding. Some countries have decided to regulate such plants like conventionally bred ones, while others treat them in the same way as earlier modified crops. Mehta argues that regulation should be based on the characteristics of the plant rather than the method used to produce it, a view shared by many scientists but not by all regulators. The disagreement matters because regulatory costs can be high enough to keep small developers out of the field.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Public attitudes have been slow to change, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them as simple ignorance. People who oppose modified crops often do so for reasons that are not about safety at all: a preference for traditional methods, concern about corporate control of food, or a belief that nature should not be altered in this way. These are values rather than factual claims, and evidence about safety, however strong, does not address them. Achterberg concedes that scientists have sometimes communicated as though every objection were a misunderstanding. Communication that treats disagreement as ignorance is unlikely to persuade anybody.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: A reasonable conclusion is that the question in the title cannot be answered with a simple yes or no. Some modified crops have delivered real benefits, others have created problems that better management could have avoided, and the most important concerns relate to ownership and regulation rather than to the plants themselves. Judging each crop by what it does, who controls it and who benefits from it would lead to more useful decisions than treating genetic modification as a single choice to be made once and for all. That approach is slower and less satisfying than a verdict, but it is closer to the evidence.
paragraphs.label: H

items.quote: can produce results that are indistinguishable from those of conventional breeding

explanation.ru: Результаты новых методов сравнимы с обычной селекцией, но прогноза о её замене нет → NOT GIVEN.
